about: Aldeigjuborg (Staraya Ladoga on the Volkhov), one port, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/aldeigjuborg.md, realms/rus.md and peoples/baltic_east.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. Three people carry the ids the neighbouring ports already tie to: aldeigjuborg.fur_buyer is Vigmund the dealer, aldeigjuborg.fur_dealer is Ihalempi who speaks for the trappers, aldeigjuborg.skald is Hallstein the host; the sites aldeigjuborg.quay and aldeigjuborg.market are likewise named as the neighbours' stories name them. Seven of the eight people are invented: no one is named here by any writer before 839. In speech the place is Aldeigja and nobody says 'Rus' before 839. (?) = not checked on a page that was opened; 'late' = told only in the kings' sagas of about 1220-1230.

ports.summary: A cluster of log houses and workshops on the left bank of a brown river, twelve kilometres up from a lake as wide as a sea, where a small river runs in and makes a harbour. It is the last place a sea ship can lie: above it the river breaks over rock, and everything goes on by river boat and other men's leave. A merchant comes for furs, wax and honey out of the woods and for thin silver with writing on it out of the south, and he brings blades, beads, cloth and a scale.
ports.seasons: The river is ice from about the first snows of early winter until some weeks after the spring equinox, and the lake shore a month longer; in that time the furs come in over the snow on sledges. Boats leave when the ice breaks, the sea ships come from midsummer, and the silver comes back down the river before the frost. Nobody who means to sail home stays past the first cold nights.

history.text: The oldest timber of the place is felled. The first settlers are Northmen, perhaps Gotlanders, in three big houses with a hearth in the middle, and one of them is a smith.
history.source: Tree-ring dates and the excavations of the Earthen Fort ground (Ravdonikas, Kirpichnikov, Ryabinin; Kuzmin's scheme), as in en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga' and ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 1, 2

history.text: In the 760s the first Norse colony ends. People from the south who build log cabins take the site, and from about now Slavs are the larger part of those who live here.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; dossier 1, 5

history.text: A bead-maker's shop begins work in the 780s, making glass eye beads by a low-heat method learned from the Arab lands. It works until the end of the 830s, and its beads buy furs.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; de.wikipedia 'Staraja Ladoga'; dossier 2, 4

history.text: A small hoard of the caliphs' silver is put in the ground here; its youngest coin is of this year. These are the oldest such coins in the lands of the eastern rivers.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; riddles_793.json rw_hoard_ladoga; dossier 4

history.text: A trading place forty years old of two to four hectares and fewer than a hundred people: Slav and Finnic householders, Northmen coming and going with the season. No writer names a ruler, a toll or a law for it.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; Design/content/audit/ports.md; dossier 1, 8

history.text: Men who call their people Rhos come to the emperor Louis at Ingelheim by way of Constantinople, and prove to be Svear. It is the first time the name is written. Nobody in this town was called that before.
history.source: Annals of St Bertin, year 839; chronicle_793.json 839-05-18-rhos-envoys; realms/rus.md

history.text: About this year an enemy burns the town, and much of it lies empty for some twenty-five years. Northmen hold it from about now and settle the left bank of the small river. Who burned it is not known.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; dossier 5, 8

history.text: Danes sent east from Birka by the casting of lots sack an unnamed town of the Slavs and come home rich. Some think it was this one (?).
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 19 (tr. Robinson 1921), not re-read (?); realms/rus.md; dossier 5

history.text: The chronicle of Kiev's year for Rurik, called from over the sea to rule. Most copies make this town his first seat; the Laurentian copy says Novgorod. The tale is partly legend (?).
history.source: Primary Chronicle 6370 (= 862), written about 1113; chronicle_793.json 862-rurik-ladoga; dossier 3, 8

history.text: Between 863 and 871 the town is burned to the ground. It is rebuilt with more Norse things in it than before, Thor's hammers among them.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; dossier 5

history.text: In the 870s a wooden fort is raised on the point between the small river and the great one. Only from now does the Norse name with 'fort' in it fit the place.
history.source: Kirpichnikov's reading, as in ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога' and 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 1, 2

history.text: A big house in the Norse manner is built, read by its diggers as an inn for merchants. A stick cut with runes lay by it.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; the rune stick found 1950 (de.wikipedia 'Staraja Ladoga'); that it carries verse is not checked (?); dossier 2, 7

history.text: About this year a very large new building goes up, perhaps of two floors, as the trade grows.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 2

history.text: About this year a stone fort replaces the wooden one: flagstone laid without mortar, walls some eight metres high with a fighting walk, and a loading hatch seven metres up the river wall.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 2

history.text: The Novgorod chronicle's year for the death of Oleg, and its word that his mound is at Ladoga. Kiev's chronicle says 912 and shows a grave of its own (?).
history.source: Novgorod First Chronicle 6430 (= 922); Primary Chronicle 6420 (= 912); ru.wikipedia 'Олегова могила (Ладога)'; dossier 3, 7

history.text: About now the town's best years end. Novgorod grows up two hundred kilometres up the river, and this place becomes its gate to the sea.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; realms/rus.md; dossier 5

history.text: Jarl Eirik Hakonarson takes and burns the fort after a long siege. His skald Eyjolf praises the burning about 1010, and the burnt layer was found in the 1980s. The year is the sagas' (?).
history.source: Eyjólfr dáðaskáld, Bandadrápa (about 1010); en.wikipedia 'Eric Haakonsson'; ru.wikipedia 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 5, 7

history.text: In the early 1000s a wooden fort stands again, behind a ditch cut from the small river to the great one.
history.source: ru.wikipedia 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 2

history.text: Yaroslav gives the men of Novgorod a written law: a merchant's life is worth forty grivnas, the same as a retainer's, and a man from over the sea clears himself by his oath alone.
history.source: Novgorod First Chronicle 6524 (= 1016); chronicle_793.json 1016-yaroslav-pravda; realms/rus.md (the wording not re-read (?))

history.text: Ingigerd, daughter of Olof of the Svear, marries Yaroslav and has this town for her bride-gift. Her father's cousin, Jarl Ragnvald Ulfsson, holds it for her from the summer (late).
history.source: Heimskringla, the saga of Olaf Haraldsson (about 1230: late); en.wikipedia 'Ragnvald Ulfsson' and 'Ingegerd Olofsdotter of Sweden'; dossier 3, 5

history.text: Olaf Haraldsson of Norway comes through into exile at Yaroslav's court and leaves his son Magnus there; Harald Sigurdsson comes east about 1031 and sails home from here about 1045 (late).
history.source: Heimskringla (late); realms/rus.md; dossier 3, 5

history.text: Ingigerd dies on 10 February. Her jarls are gone from the town by now, and it is held again from Novgorod.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Ingegerd Olofsdotter of Sweden'; realms/rus.json who_holds (the end of the jarldom about 1045 is a reckoning (?)); dossier 3, 5

eras.text: A small place with no lord. Log cabins of the Slavs on the bank of the small river, a bead-maker's shop, a smith who also casts bronze, a barn of emmer, and one house bigger than the rest where a Svea dealer weighs silver. Men from the woods bring skins and stand apart. An older Slav fort watches the river two kilometres below. You deal with whoever sits in the biggest house, and nobody takes a toll.

The town has been burned and half of it is nettles. Northmen hold what stands and build along the left bank of the small river; they take skins from the people of the woods as tribute and call it peace. The bead shop is gone. Fewer sea ships come, and those that do ask at the river mouth who is master this year before they row up.

Ash. The town was burned to the ground and nothing has been raised but a few lean-tos against charred posts. There is nobody to weigh with. Men dig in the black earth for what their fathers hid, and a ship that comes for furs finds trappers who do not know whom to sell to. Stay away, or come with timber and food.

Rebuilt, and more Norse than it ever was. A wooden fort stands on the point between the two rivers; from 881 a big house takes in merchants, and about 894 a larger one goes up. Men wear small iron hammers at the neck. New silver is scarce for a generation, and the trade is in furs, cut silver and trust. The lord's men sit in the fort and are named to you at the landing.

The best years. A stone fort of dry-laid flagstone stands on the point with a hatch high in the river wall for hoisting goods. Heavy new silver comes up the rivers by the sackful, and with it glazed pots that shine like metal. The prince sits far away in Kiev and his men at Holmgard take what is his. Mounds stand tall along both banks, and the dead on the far side are burned.

Still a harbour, no longer the market. The furs are bought up the river at Novgorod and the tribute comes in to fixed stations; this town loads what Novgorod has already sold. The silver from the south grows thinner each year. After 988 the prince's men are Christians of the Greek rite, though no church is known here.

Jarl Eirik's men burned the stone fort in 997 and harried the coast for some summers. A wooden fort is raised again behind a new ditch. The silver now is pennies of the English and the Germans. In the brothers' wars after 1015 the harbour is full of hired fighting men going up to Novgorod, and any ship that carries them is well paid.

The town is the bride-gift of the Svea princess Ingigerd and is held for her by a Svea jarl, Ragnvald, and after him his son Eilif (late). Norse is spoken in the fort and Slavic in the houses. Kings out of Norway pass through, in flight or coming home rich. The law of Novgorod runs here for a stranger, and the jarl's word besides.

Novgorod's sea-gate, held by the prince's governor. Christians are laid without mounds on the far bank. Silver is bars and western pennies; the furs go west in Gotland ships. In the winter of 1066 to 1067 Novgorod itself is burned from Polotsk and its bells are hauled away on sledges, and the news comes down the ice.

sites.name: The mouth of the small river
sites.see: A narrow side river running into a broad brown one under a low bank of clay. Sea ships lie nose to the mud with their masts down, and beyond them flat-bottomed river boats and dugouts are drawn up in a row. Log houses stand close behind, grey smoke lying flat over them. Wet clay, tar, wood smoke and the sour smell of raw skins; a hammer somewhere, and a tongue you do not know.
sites.source: The mouth and channels of the Ladozhka are the harbour, on the left bank of the Volkhov, about 12 km from the lake; the first houses on the Ladozhka's right bank (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 1). Brown water (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md). No toll is known here, so none is taken (audit/ports.md). The card is the silver road's step 6 (chain_silver_road_793.json).

sites.name: The trading bank
sites.see: A strip of trodden ground between the houses and the water. Skins lie in tied bundles of forty, stacked like firewood: squirrel, marten, beaver, a few black fox. Cakes of yellow wax the size of a quern, honey in birch-bark tubs, sacks of emmer. Men in fur caps from the woods stand a little apart with a woman who speaks for them. No booths, no stalls: a blanket on the ground and a scale held up to the light.
sites.source: No market square is recorded: this open ground is the game's guess (?) (dossier 8). Furs above all, bought with beads; wax, honey and captives out, silver, beads, blades and amber in (dossier 4). Furs counted by the timber of forty and marten skins reckoned as money are from later usage (peoples/baltic_east.md 5 (?)). Emmer: the burned barn of the 700s, 80 parts emmer to 20 of soft wheat (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога').

sites.name: The biggest house
sites.see: One long house among the cabins, built the old Northern way with a hearth down the middle and benches at the walls. A broad man sits near the door where the light is, a folding scale in front of him and a leather bag of thin white coins at his knee. Bundles of skins hang from the rafters out of reach of the dogs. Behind the house, a pen of split logs roofed at one end, and somebody coughing in it.
sites.source: The 'big houses' with a central hearth are those of the first Norse settlers (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'); that one is still a dealer's house in 793 is the game's guess (?). 'Deal with whoever sits in the biggest house' (realms/rus.json who_holds). The dealer Vigmund and the pen are the silver road chain's (chain_silver_road_793.json steps 6, 7, 12, 14); captives as a thing sold east (dossier 4).

sites.name: The bead-maker's shop
sites.see: A low cabin with its door propped open for the heat. Inside, a small clay hearth no bigger than a cooking fire, an iron rod, and a woman turning a blob of dark glass on the rod's end while she lays a thread of yellow round it. Finished beads hang drying on a line of bast like berries: blue, green, black, each with a ring of white and a dot, so that it looks back at you. Hot glass, singed hair.
sites.source: The bead-maker's shop of the 780s to the end of the 830s, making glass eye beads by an Arab low-heat method; the beads bought furs (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; de.wikipedia 'Staraja Ladoga'; dossier 2, 4). The maker and how she learned are invented.

sites.name: The old workshop
sites.see: The oldest roof in the place, black with sixty winters of soot. A stone-lined forge, a block with an anvil let into it, tongs and hammers of a dozen sizes hung in order on pegs, and clay moulds stacked by the wall. On a shelf above the door sits a bronze man the length of a finger, with two curved horns rising from his head and meeting above it. Charcoal, hot iron, and the hiss of the quenching tub.
sites.source: The Scandinavian workshop of the 750s in the oldest layer, with a smith's tool hoard (some 26 pieces is not checked (?)) and the small bronze finial of a man with a horned head-dress in the Vendel style, called 'the singing Odin'; casting moulds (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 2, 7). The horns are a head-dress on a figure: nobody wore such a helmet. That a smith works the same ground through every age is the game's simplification (?).

sites.name: The fort at the Lyubsha mouth
sites.see: The first thing a skipper passes: on the right bank, two kilometres below the town, a rampart of stone and earth with a palisade on top, standing over the mouth of a stream. Boats lie under it, and men on the wall watch you go by without waving. Smoke from a few roofs inside. Each year the stream's mouth is a little siltier and the boats lie a little further out.
sites.source: The Lyubsha fort: built about 700 by Slavs on an older Finnic palisaded site, a stone-and-earth rampart, over 1,000 finds with ship rivets, moulds and both Norse and local arrowheads; given up in the later 800s as the lake fell and the Lyubsha silted (ru.wikipedia 'Любшанская крепость', after Ryabinin's digs from 1997; dossier 1, 2). That the river pilots live here is invented.

sites.name: The river-boat bank below the rocks
sites.see: Above the last houses the river narrows between limestone banks, and from the bend comes a steady noise like wind in pines: the first of the rapids. Here the river boats load. Long shallow hulls and dugouts widened with a plank a side, men up to the thigh in brown water passing bales hand to hand, a line of porters going up the bank path with wax on their shoulders. Nothing with a keel goes further.
sites.source: Sea ships stop here and goods go on by river boat (de.wikipedia 'Staraja Ladoga'; Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md); rapids above the town, hard at low water, drowned by the dam of 1926 (en.wikipedia 'Volkhov (river)'; dossier 1). River pilots are a fair inference, not a find (dossier 3). Counts toward unlock_pilot_volkhov (unlocks_793.json).

sites.name: The posts on the bank
sites.see: A little way from the houses, where the bank is highest, a tall post stands in the ground with a face cut in it, and smaller posts round it. Bread, an onion, a strip of dried meat and a bowl lie at its foot, and the dogs have been at them. No roof and no fence. A trader with his cap in his hand is talking to the big post in a low voice, as a man talks to a creditor.
sites.source: No temple or holy place is recorded here: this one is invented (?) (dossier 8), after what an envoy of the caliph saw among the Rus traders on the Volga in 922, who laid bread, meat, onions and drink before a tall wooden post and asked it for a buyer with much silver who would not haggle (Ibn Fadlan, in paraphrase only: realms/rus.md scene 4; peoples/baltic_east.md 4). Heathen through the 800s and 900s, Thor's hammers after 865 (dossier 6). After 988 nobody swears by the old gods in the prince's towns.

sites.name: The tall mounds
sites.see: Along the river below the town stand steep round hills too regular to be hills, grass-grown, the tallest as high as five men and seen from the water long before the roofs. Nobody builds near them. Cattle graze the lower slopes and will not go to the top. From the tallest you can see the river both ways, the far grave-field, and on a clear day a pale line that is the lake.
sites.source: The sopki, the tall mounds along the Volkhov. One, about 10 m high, is called Oleg's Grave: a third of it was dug in 1820 and gave burnt bone, a two-barbed spearhead of the 700s or early 800s and iron scraps, so it is older than the prince it is named for (ru.wikipedia 'Олегова могила (Ладога)'; dossier 2, 7). The riddle r-gest-24 and the small hoard rw_hoard_ladoga (riddles_793.json) belong to this ground.

sites.name: The Northmen's street and the big house
sites.see: A plank-laid lane along the left bank of the small river, houses gable-end to the water, each with its boat below. Halfway along stands a house twice the length of the others with a carved door-post and a bench outside worn hollow. Inside, a long fire, sleeping benches with men's sea chests under them, a tafl board scratched on a plank, and a host who knows what ship each chest came off. Fish, wet wool, ale.
sites.source: Varangian Street (Varyazhskaya) on the left bank of the Ladozhka, settled by the Northmen who took the town about the 830s-840s; the 'big house' of 881, read as a merchants' inn, with a rune stick beside a large Norse-style house; a very large building about 894 (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'; dossier 2). In its early 900s layers: lustre pottery from Mesopotamia and a birch-bark roll with a ship drawn on it. Before 881 the lodging is an ordinary house on the lane (invented).

sites.name: The grave-field on the far bank
sites.see: Across the great river, on a low terrace opposite the town, a dozen small mounds in rough grass. On some the turf is new and the ground round them is black with a pyre's ash; boat rivets lie rusting where a hull was burned. At the edge one mound is larger and has a timber chamber under it. In later years flat graves without mounds lie beside them, heads to the west.
sites.source: Plakun: thirteen mounds counted in 1940, in use about 850 to 950 (Mikhailov: only from the 900s); the early graves cremations; Mound 11 a chamber grave of a man of 60 to 70 with a horse, perhaps a Christian; at least five incomers from the Mälar country by strontium; unmounded Christian graves of the 1000s-1100s (ru.wikipedia 'Плакун (урочище)' and 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 2, 6). Boat rivets in some mounds are not checked (?).

sites.name: The fort on the point
sites.see: On the tongue of land between the small river and the great one: in the 870s a palisade and a gate; from about 900 a wall of grey flagstone laid dry, eight metres high, with men walking the top and a square hatch far up the river face where a beam swings out to hoist bales from a boat below. After the burning of 997 it is timber again behind a ditch, and the old stone shows black at its foot.
sites.source: The wooden fort of the 870s on the point between Ladozhka and Volkhov (Kirpichnikov); the stone fort of about 900, flagstone without mortar, walls about 8 m, a fighting walk 2 m wide and a loading hatch 7 m up the river wall; broken in 997; wood again in the early 1000s behind a ditch (ru.wikipedia 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 2). No toll is known at any time (dossier 4): the lord's men take gifts, not a tenth. hear_law and lawsuit are true only from 1016, under Novgorod's law (realms/rus.md).

people.name: Vigmund
people.trait: The man in the biggest house. No lord and no king's man: he is simply the one with the scale, the silver and the pen behind the wall, and everyone in the place owes him something.
people.want: Sword blades, more than he can get, and a second road west for his silver so that Birka does not name every price.
people.fear: A lord. Any lord: the day somebody with forty armed men decides the place needs one, his scale is only a scale.
people.voice: Slow and friendly, with long silences he is happy to sit in. Names a weight, never a price. Calls every man 'friend' and means that the tally is open.
people.looks: About fifty, broad and heavy, a grey-fair beard combed and a fur-lined cap he wears indoors, a belted coat with silver-wire trim, a folding scale on a cord at his neck and three rings on a hand missing its smallest finger.
knows: what a timber of marten, beaver or squirrel weighs out to in white silver this season
who came down the river this year and what they brought: he sees every boat
what the silver is paid for in the south, which is people, and what a sound young one fetches
that the white coins come from men who allow no images and want no wine, by way of a king on a great river who takes a tenth
which Svea skippers are in the harbour and which of them can be trusted with a debt over the winter

ties.note: Holmfast brings him hiltless blades each summer and takes furs and silver home; neither has ever caught the other short, and both have tried
the smith fits hilts to his blades and mends his scales, and is paid late
she stands between him and the trappers, and takes one skin in twenty for it; he would like to buy at the trap
bought the boy for his tallying and taught him the weights; says he never had a better hand and never told him so
some of the people in the pen came from Budimir's river; nothing has been said, and nothing will be forgotten
the Gotlanders come east without asking Birka, sell beads of their own and bury what they earn; he cannot tell what they have
once offered Holmfast a timber of sable for his English tally-boy and was refused; he still thinks the price was fair
a fowler of the Svear's country traps for him in winter and sends the best skins east by Holmfast's ship; Vigmund pays a year late, in silver nobody at home has seen
advanced her a season's glass and is paid in beads, every one of them counted in front of him

lines.greet: A new boat. Sit, friend. Nobody takes a toll here. I only like to know what comes up my river. Now, what is under that sailcloth?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian. I told them it was your boat when she was still a speck. Sit where you sat before. The scale has missed you.
rumour: The silver was thin this year. They say the king on the great river took more than his tenth. Skins are cheap, so buy now and say nothing.
A Gotlander came across the lake alone, no Svea with him, in a night calm. A fine seaman, or a lucky one. I want to know which.
Bring me blades. Bare, no hilts, the kind with the pattern in the iron. For those I pay the white silver, and I do not make you wait.
The woodsmen say the winter will be long. They are always right about winter and always wrong about what their skins are worth.
lines.saying: A man with a scale has no friends on the day he weighs. He has them all the day after.
lines.farewell: Go before the cold nights. The lake does not care what you paid for the cargo. Come back when the ice goes.

people.source: invented: the dealer of the silver road chain (chain_silver_road_793.json steps 6, 7, 12, 14; Design/content/chains/silver_road.md), given a life here. The name is Vig- + -mund (names_placeholder.json). No ruler is named before 839 (dossier 1, 3); the 'king on the great river who takes a tenth' is the Khazar king at Itil, never named in speech (realms/rus.md). The dealer who pays in the caliphs' silver and wants swords is the spine's hook (silver_road).

people.name: Milava
people.trait: The bead-maker. Makes eye beads on a small fire by a way no one north of here knows, and understands exactly what that is worth: a marten skin a bead in a good winter.
people.want: Glass to melt: broken cups, window scraps, cakes of raw glass, anything from the Rhine. And one apprentice who will not carry the trick to Birka.
people.fear: Fire in the thatch. And cheaper beads from the west arriving by the sack.
people.voice: Quick and sharp, never looks up from the rod. Asks a question, answers it herself, and then asks whether she was right.
people.looks: A little over thirty, thin, strong-wristed, fair hair bound under a linen cloth, eyebrows half singed away, a grey shift with the sleeves tied back and a string of her own worst beads round her neck.
knows: what beads buy in the woods, colour by colour: blue for marten, green for squirrel, the black with yellow eyes for nearly anything
glass: which broken western cup melts clean and which turns to grey slag
every woman's news in the place, because every woman passes her door
that she learned the low fire from a man who came up the river from the south and went back; she will not say more

ties.note: Ihalempi tells her which colours the woods want this winter, and gets first choice of the string
he advanced her a season's glass; she pays in beads and counts every one she gives him
has never met Ragnvi, the Birka bead-maker, and knows her work on sight: too much lead, the eyes crooked
sells him beads by the string of forty, counted twice by him and once more by her
beads from the western beach markets reach the lake in Gotland boats; she buys one of each kind and breaks it to see how it was made
he makes her rods and she lets him use her fire for small bronze; they argue all day and neither would work elsewhere
pushed bread through the pen wall to the Frisian boy his first winter; he keeps her accounts for nothing

lines.greet: Stand out of my light. Are you buying or looking? Looking, I think. Have you glass? Broken will do. Then you are buying.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the broken cups. Was I right about the green? I was. The woods took every one. Bring more of that glass.
rumour: One of my eye beads bought a marten skin last winter. One. The man who told me was angry, because he had paid two.
Far south, they say, a bead like mine buys a person. I do not ask where my beads go after the woods. I make them round.
The big man wants the trappers to come to his door and not Ihalempi's blanket. They will not. They have seen what is behind his house.
lines.saying: Glass is sand that remembers the fire. So do I, and so does my thatch.
lines.farewell: Go on. And if you see a Birka bead, look at the eye. Crooked. Tell them I said so.

people.source: invented. The shop is real: glass eye beads by an Arab low-heat method, 780s to the end of the 830s; the beads bought furs (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 2, 4). 'A bead for a slave' is a 10th-century Arab traveller's word, cited by the Russian page, and Ibn Fadlan's dirham a bead on the Volga is not checked (?) (dossier 4): both later than her, so she has it only as hearsay. The name is Mil- with a short woman's ending, after later Slavic names (?).

people.name: Audvald
people.trait: Smith and bronze-caster in the oldest workshop, grandson of the Gotlander who first lit its forge. Fits northern hilts to bare Frankish blades and keeps his grandfather's tools in the order he found them.
people.want: Bar iron and good blades to work on, and somebody who will listen to a riddle to the end before answering.
people.fear: That he is the last Gotlander in a town that has forgotten Gotlanders built it.
people.voice: Dry and unhurried. Says a thing once. Likes to set a question and go on hammering while you think.
people.looks: Past forty, lean and stooped from the anvil, a long plaited fair beard tucked into his belt away from the fire, a leather apron, burn scars to the elbow, and a small iron ring on a thong that he turns when he is thinking.
knows: blades: which have the pattern in the iron and which only look it, and where the good ones are made, though he has never seen the place
how to mend a rivet, a rudder iron or a kettle while the ship waits
what his grandfather said of the first three houses, and why the first Northmen left in the 760s (they were too few, he says, and it is all he says)
riddles: he has the one of the corpse on a corpse, and tells it only when the river ice is in his mind
what the little horned bronze man on his shelf is for: it was the top of something, and it sang when the first smith struck it (?)

ties.note: his father's brother's line still works iron on Gotland; a Gute skipper carries word between them every second summer
two casters at two ends of the Svear's sea who have never met; Holmfast carries their opinions of each other's weights to and fro
hilts the blades Holmfast brings bare, for a share paid in iron
sat a bench with Ravn one winter on Gotland long ago; the riddle he gives is one Ravn will know the wording of
works for the big house and is paid late; keeps a tally stick of it by the forge where Vigmund can see it
makes her glass rods; she tells him his bronze is too thick

lines.greet: A Frisian boat. Then you have rivets working loose and do not know it yet. Sit. I will tell you which when I have looked.
lines.greet_again: You again. The rudder iron held, then. I said it would. People are always surprised, and I never know why.
rumour: Holmfast brings the blades bare so nobody at home sees what he carries. I put the hilts on. After that they are nobody's business but the buyer's.
My grandfather built this roof. Three houses and a forge, and all Northmen. Then the log-cabin people came. They stayed; we mostly did not.
One spring I saw a thing go down on the ice. A corpse sitting on a corpse. Say what it was and I will say where to dig.
lines.saying: Iron tells you at the first blow what it will be. Men take longer and are wrong more often.
lines.farewell: Keep her rivets tight. And think about the corpse on the corpse. The river will remind you.

people.source: invented. The workshop and its tool hoard are real, in the oldest layer of the 750s; the first settlers were perhaps Gotlanders (Ryabinin), and their colony ended in the 760s (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 1, 2). The bronze finial with the horned head-dress, 'the singing Odin', is real; that it sang is his own tale (?). Hilts fitted in the north to Frankish blades: the spine (swords_north: Birka before 901). His riddle is r-gest-24 (riddles_793.json: given at aldeigjuborg, reward rw_hoard_ladoga). The name is Aud- + -vald, both common on Gotland's later stones (?).

people.name: Budimir
people.trait: River pilot, of the fort at the stream mouth below the town. Knows the lake's south shore by the colour of the water and the rapids by their sound, and has never lost a boat he was paid for.
people.want: Fair pay in things that keep: iron, salt, cloth. And his sister's son back from wherever the big house sold him.
people.fear: The lake in an onshore wind. And the stream at his own fort, which silts a little more every spring.
people.voice: Speaks Norse in short pieces with the words in his own order. Points more than he talks. Laughs suddenly and seldom.
people.looks: Forty or so, short and very wide in the shoulder, brown beard, a belted shirt of undyed linen to the knee, bast shoes, a sounding pole taller than himself and a wooden charm on a cord.
knows: the way in across the lake: where the shoals lie on the south shore, and which sky means go back
the river from the lake to the rocks, and from the rocks up, where goods are carried on the bank at low water
that far up, where the river leaves the upper lake, it sometimes runs backwards for days; he has seen it and expects not to be believed
when the ice will go, within three days, by the sound it makes at night
who was taken from the upper river and by whom

ties.note: his wife is her mother's sister; the Finnic and the Slav houses at the stream mouth have married each other for three generations
his sister's son went into the pen and south; he pilots Vigmund's ships at the full price and looks at the water while he does it
brings the Gotland boats over the lake without a Svea aboard, and is paid in salt
has piloted Holmfast's ship up the river every summer for ten years; they have never eaten together
Svea skippers tell him their own pilot at home reads water better; he asks whether their water has rocks in it
the Frisian boy asked him the river's names in Slavic and wrote them on a stick; nobody had asked before

lines.greet: You draw too much water. Not for the river: for the lake shore. Next time, come in behind me. Now you pay, now I show.
lines.greet_again: Frisian. The boat is whole. Good. You listened, or the lake was asleep. Which? No matter. Same price.
rumour: Up where the river is born it runs backwards some years. Into its own lake. Three days, four. I saw it. You do not believe. Good, cheaper for me.
The stream at our wall fills with mud. My father tied his boat at the gate. I tie mine forty steps out. My son will walk.
The ice sang last night. Thin song. Twelve days and it goes, or I give you back the iron.
lines.saying: The lake drowns the proud. The river drowns the hurried. The man who is both does not need a pilot, he needs a mound.
lines.farewell: Go at dawn, when the lake is flat. Wind after noon. If the water turns white ahead, turn left and pray to whoever you have.

people.source: invented. River pilots for the rapids are a fair inference, not a find (dossier 3). The Lyubsha fort, Slav on an older Finnic site, silting and given up in the later 800s (ru.wikipedia 'Любшанская крепость'); the lake's shoals and waves (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md); the upper Volkhov can reverse (en.wikipedia 'Volkhov (river)'); ice from late November to early April (dossier 1). He teaches unlock_pilot_volkhov (unlocks_793.json). The name is Bud- + -mir, after later Slavic names (?): no ordinary Slav of the Volkhov is named in the period (names_placeholder.json).

people.name: Ihalempi
people.trait: She speaks for the trappers. Finnic by her mother, raised at the stream-mouth fort, with Slavic and Norse enough to count in both: no skin from the woods is sold on the bank without her blanket under it.
people.want: That the men of the woods are paid what a skin is worth at Birka, less the journey, and know it.
people.fear: That the Northmen will stop buying and start taking. She has heard how it goes on other rivers.
people.voice: Quiet and even. Translates exactly, then adds what the trapper did not say. Counts aloud in three tongues so that nobody can claim he misheard.
people.looks: Under thirty, small and straight-backed, black hair in one plait, a dark woollen dress with bronze spirals sewn along the apron hem, a knife and a bag of tally sticks at her belt, and a string of Milava's best beads.
knows: what the woods will bring in after the first snow, and which winters the squirrel is thick
the count in skins: forty to the timber, and what a timber of each kind is against cloth, iron and beads
which goods the trappers want and which they laugh at (wine; they tried it once)
who among the buyers gives short measure, in order
that there is no market in the woods, no town and no king: you go with someone they know, or you do not go

ties.note: tells her the colours the woods want; wears the proof round her neck
her mother's sister's husband; she grew up in his house
he wants her out from between him and the furs; she wants him to weigh in front of the people he buys from
the one Svea who counts aloud as she does; she lets him count twice and he lets her check
the old Gotland trader of the Curonian coast sends amber here that was refused there; she has learned to ask where a thing was last offered
Botbjorn of Gotland buys through her blanket and not at the big house; she keeps the dark sables back for him, and he brings the woods iron
a Wend who buys wax sent her a comb by a Svea ship, having heard that a woman on the Volkhov sets the wax price; she has not decided what he wants
in the chain's first years a young Gotland steersman is given the second-best skins at her blanket, which is an honour at his age

lines.greet: They ask who you are and what you carry. I told them: a stranger, with cloth. They ask to feel the cloth. That is a good sign.
lines.greet_again: The men remember your cloth. It lasted the winter. They brought the better skins down for you, and I did not tell them to.
rumour: Squirrel will be thick this winter. The cones were heavy. Buy your beads now, green ones, before the big house hears it.
A trapper asked why the white silver has scratches and no face. I said the men who make it have a god who dislikes faces. He approved.
On other rivers the Northmen take a skin from each hearth and call it peace. Here they still pay. I count every summer that they do.
lines.saying: Forty skins is forty in every tongue. It is only the price that needs translating.
lines.farewell: They say: come after the snow, when the fur is winter fur. I say: come anyway. I will keep some back.

people.source: invented. Finnic people lived on this river before Slav or Northman, and the Lyubsha fort stands on a Finnic site (dossier 1, 2); furs are bought with beads (dossier 4); 'Finland has furs and no market: go with a Swede' and tribute of 'a squirrel-skin and a beaver-skin from each hearth' in 859 (peoples/baltic_east.md 5, 12; Primary Chronicle 6367 (?)). Bronze spirals on the apron: Luistari, not checked (?). No Finnic woman of the period is named: the name is built from the old stems Iha (joy) and Lempi (love) (fi.wikipedia 'Suomen muinaisnimet' (?)). No woman go-between is recorded (?).

people.name: Folkbern
people.trait: A Frisian ship's boy of Wijnaldum, taken off the Danish coast and sold east for his tallying. If the house bought him out, he is its own man on the Volkhov: free, baptised, fluent in three tongues, and the only person here who remembers the tide.
people.want: To be worth what was paid for him, to the last ounce, and to hear Frisian spoken once a year.
people.fear: The pen behind the big house, which he passes every day. And that he is forgetting his mother's face.
people.voice: Careful and exact, a clerk's manner learned from a scale. Slips into Frisian mid-sentence when he is glad. Never raises his voice.
people.looks: As a man: thirty, slight, fair hair cut short, a clean grey tunic of Frisian cloth kept for the day your boat comes, a tally stick behind his ear, a small wooden cross under his shirt and a rope scar on his neck.
knows: every weight and every debt in the place: he cut the notches for half of them
the price of furs here against Birka and Dorestad, which he works out on a stick while you watch
Norse well and Slavic usefully, and the count in skins
which of the people in the pen are Christians, and who has kin that would pay
what a Frisian house on this bank would need, down to the roof pegs

ties.note: was Vigmund's tally-boy; if freed, still weighs for him by the day and is paid for it, which both find strange
the pilot of the Wijnaldum creek is his mother's brother, and taught him to count by notching the tides
two boys who tally for Svea masters, a sea apart; a stick with a greeting cut in Latin letters went west one summer and another came back
Holmfast was the one who told the house a Frisian boy was in the pen; Folkbern reckons the debt in years, not silver
learned the river's Slavic names from him, and in return taught him to cut a tally the Frisian way
she gave him bread through the pen wall the first winter; he keeps her accounts for nothing

lines.greet: You are from the Rhine mouths. I heard it before I saw you. Say something more. Anything. Say what the weather was at home.
lines.greet_again: Master. Skins are down a tenth since you left and wax is up. I have it all on the stick. And I kept your place at the bank.
rumour: There are two in the pen who say the Our Father. English, I think, from a monastery. Vigmund does not know what that is worth. I do.
A stick came from Birka, cut in Latin letters. A boy there tallies for Holmfast. He asks if this river has a tide. I said no, God help us.
If we had our own roof here, between the big house and the forge, we would buy at the snow price and sell at the ice-break price.
lines.saying: At home the sea comes twice a day to count the land. Here nothing counts but me.
lines.farewell: Greet the mound for me. Tell my mother's brother I notch the days as he showed me. God keep the boat.

people.source: invented: the boy of the silver road chain (chain_silver_road_793.json step 7; Design/content/chains/silver_road.md). He is a person to speak with from step 7; he is the house's factor only after the ending end_ransom (the flag unlock_factor_aldeigjuborg). No Frisian is known this far east in 793 (dossier 8): he is here because he was sold, not because Frisians came. The ransom of captives as a good work: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 15, 35 (not re-read (?)). The name is Folk- + -bern. He dies before the burning of about 840.

people.name: Hallstein
people.trait: Keeper of the big house on the Northmen's street, built the year he came, and a maker of verses when the ale is in. Feeds and beds every merchant who rows up the river, buys their furs, and holds their chests, their quarrels and their messages over the winter.
people.want: A full house in summer, guests who pay before they go up the river and not after, and verses he has not heard.
people.fear: Fire. He was a boy when the town burned to the ground, and he dug in the ash with his father.
people.voice: Loud, easy, a host's voice. Remembers what you drank. Goes quiet and exact when the talk turns to who owes whom.
people.looks: Near forty, tall and thick-set, a red-fair beard, a blue tunic with tablet-woven trim and wide eastern breeches gathered at the knee, a small iron hammer at his neck and a ring of keys on his belt.
knows: who is in the fort this year and what gift they expect of a stranger
which river convoys have come down and which have not, and what that means for the price of silver
every guest's home port, ship and debts for twenty years back
verses and riddles cut on sticks that guests have left: he can read them and likes to be asked
where in the black earth people still dig for what was hidden before the burning, and how seldom they find it

ties.note: the Svear king's skald lodged with him going east and left a stick with the riddle of the sun for a week's ale; Hallstein now says he made it himself, and Arnfast has heard
holds the Birka house's furs under his roof till the ice goes, as the dealers here held them for Holmsten's grandfather
Gotland steersmen leave silver with him over the winter and do not say how much; he does not count it, and they know that he does
Tonna of the Skane river mouth sent combs and amber east on trust and a riddle with them; he has answered the riddle and not yet sent the furs
his wife is of the old smith's line; the forge and the big house share a well and an opinion of the fort
a Halogaland man who trades walrus rope south has heard of this house from Svea skippers at Skiringssal, and sends a coil each year for the ships' gear; they have never met
the Gotlanders' skald keeps the stick before his and sends on whoever answers it; they have never met, and agree about the Svear king's poet

lines.greet: A western boat! We do not see many. Put your chest under that bench. Nobody has ever lost one in this house, and I mean to die saying so.
lines.greet_again: I know that boat's kin. Your father's chest stood under the same bench. Sit. You drink the dark ale, as he did.
rumour: The convoy from the south is late. Either the rapids down there were low, or the riders caught them. Silver will be dear until we know.
A man went through here saying he would be a merchant at Kiev. He had forty shields in the boat. I have seen merchants. They carry less iron.
A skald left me a stick for his ale. It asks who lights all lands and is chased by wolves. Answer it, and you drink free.
lines.saying: A guest brings news and takes news. A good host makes sure it is not the same news.
lines.farewell: Go down on the morning calm. If the lake is white, come back: the bench is paid till the new moon.

people.source: invented. The 'big house' of 881, read as a merchants' inn, with a rune stick beside it; Varangian Street; the burning of about 865; Thor's hammers after it (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 2, 5, 6). His riddle is r-gest-15, the sun, of the set dellings_door, found here from 871 (riddles_793.json; spine riddle_road). The man with forty shields is Oleg's taking of Kiev in the guise of merchants, by the chronicle's 882 (?) (realms/rus.md scene 3). Wide breeches: Ibn Rusta on the Rus, about 903-913, not re-read (?). The name is Hall- + -stein. After his death the house has a host in each age (the role re-forges).

people.name: Ragnvald Ulfsson
people.trait: A jarl of the Gauts and a cousin of King Olof of the Svear, who came east with the king's daughter Ingigerd and holds the town as her bride-gift (late). His son Eilif is jarl after him. An old hand at standing between two kings without being crushed.
people.want: The harbour quiet, the princess's dues paid, and the furs moving. And honest word from the west, where he has enemies and kin.
people.fear: That the burning of 997 is the kind of thing that happens twice. He counts every longship on the lake.
people.voice: Courteous, a little weary, exact about rank. Asks after the kings of the west one by one, as a man asks after neighbours.
people.looks: Sixty or near it, tall, grey hair cut to the collar and a trimmed beard, a red cloak pinned at the shoulder with a gold ring-pin, a silver cross on a chain over a coat of eastern cut, and a sword he does not take off indoors.
knows: the law a stranger stands under here since 1016: his oath alone clears him, and his life is worth forty grivnas
what the princess Ingigerd is owed from the town, and that he takes gifts and no tenth
who is at Yaroslav's court this year: which king's son, which exile, which hired captain
the west: Olof of the Svear, Olaf of Norway and the Danes' king, each of whom he has dealt with and one of whom he had to leave
when hired men are wanted up the river, and what a ship that carries them is paid

ties.note: a Svea who has been to England and come home with its silver is a man he sends for when he wants to know what Cnut's pennies are worth
Cnut's reach in the north is the reason careful men of the Svear keep a harbour in the east; he asks every western skipper what Cnut is doing
knows of Thorkell the Tall as every northern lord does: a man who changed kings and prospered; he would like to hear from a western skipper how that ended
the big house on the Northmen's street lodges his guests and the kings' sons who pass; its host of the day answers to him

lines.greet: You are welcome under the princess's peace. No tenth is taken here. A gift to her house is usual. Tell me first: who is king in England this year?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian house. Your word last time was true, and I acted on it. Sit by me. What is the Danes' king doing now?
rumour: They want fighting men up the river again, and pay a ship well to bring them. I do not ask what for. Brothers, usually.
The stone at the foot of this wall is black. Eirik Hakonarson did that. His skald made a poem of it. I have heard the poem.
A law is written at Novgorod. A stranger from over the sea swears alone and is believed. Do not make them regret it while I hold this town.
lines.saying: A man who serves two kings must be honest with both. It is the only thing neither expects.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and before the frost. If you meet a king's son on the lake, give him my greeting and no opinion.

people.source: historical, but told only in Heimskringla (about 1230: late): Ragnvald Ulfsson, jarl in Västergötland, cousin of Olof of the Svear, jarl of Aldeigjuborg from the summer of 1019 for Ingigerd; his sons Eilif, jarl after him, and Uleb (en.wikipedia 'Ragnvald Ulfsson'; dossier 3). His birth and death are not recorded, so both are 0; the year 1030 for his going is the game's guess (?). That he was a Christian is the saga's picture (?). Novgorod's law of 1016 (realms/rus.md). No toll is known here (dossier 4). The burning of 997 and Eyjolf's poem (dossier 5, 7). His lines are invented.

stories.title: A bead for a pelt
stories.summary: At the head of the road nothing is bought with coin. The bead-maker needs western glass to melt, the trappers want her beads, the dealer wants their furs, and the white silver sits at the end of the row. A merchant who brings broken cups from the Rhine can walk the whole row himself, if the woman who speaks for the woods will stand beside him.
stories.picture: A trodden river bank under a low white sky: a blanket on the ground with a string of blue eye beads on it, a small dark-haired woman with bronze spirals on her apron holding up four fingers to three men in fur caps, a foreign merchant beside her with a broken green glass cup in his hand, bundles of skins stacked behind.

beats.text: Your pennies are looked at and handed back. Nobody here knows the king on them. Ihalempi says the woods want beads, iron and cloth, in that order, and that the beads are made forty steps away.

Milava will not take silver either. She wants glass: broken cups, raw cakes, scraps. For a sack of it she will make a string of forty eye beads while you wait out the wind, and tell you which colour buys what.
On the Rhine broken glass is swept up and sold by the basket to the furnace men. A basket costs less than a day's bread. Nobody asks why a Frisian wants three.

A bead-maker on the Skane beach looks at one of Milava's beads for a long time, then offers you four of his own for it. He wants to know how the eye is put in without the bead cracking. You do not know.
With beads on the blanket the trappers come close. Ihalempi counts aloud in three tongues. The skins they bring out now are not the ones they showed you before.

Vigmund watches you carry marten past his door that he did not sell you. He asks, pleasantly, who taught a Frisian the bead count. Then he weighs out the first writing silver you have ever been paid in (sets sv_first_dirham).

At Birka the bead-maker Ragnvi has one of the eastern eye beads, brought back on a Gotlander's wrist. She has broken three of her own trying to make it. She would like to know what fire it is done on.

On Gotland the smith who winds beads says the eye is a trick of the hand and not of the fire, and that he could do it if he chose. He has not chosen yet. His beads go east by the hundred string all the same.

endings.how: You brought glass, had the beads made, bought from the trappers through Ihalempi and sold the furs yourself.
endings.text: Milava keeps a sack of your broken cups under her bench with your mark on it. Ihalempi lays her blanket where your boat lies. The trappers call you the glass man, and bring the winter fur down when they hear the boat is in.
endings.reward: Furs at the trappers' own price here for this merchant and his heir at half (buy_at_source); Ihalempi and Milava as friends; the thread's flag sv_first_dirham; the unlock aldeigjuborg.count_in_skins.

endings.how: You sold the glass to Vigmund, who sold it on to Milava at his own price.
endings.text: A quick profit in white silver, weighed at once. Milava pays more for her glass that year and knows why. She serves you last from then on, and Ihalempi's men bring you the skins they could not sell elsewhere.
endings.reward: Silver now, and Vigmund's good will; Milava and Ihalempi cool toward the house for two seasons; the thread's flag sv_first_dirham all the same.

endings.how: You took one of her beads to the western bead-makers and told them all you had seen of her fire.
endings.text: Two summers on, eye beads made on a Skane beach come east in Gotland boats, cheaper and nearly as good. Milava breaks one open, looks at it, and looks at you. She does not close her door. She does raise her price, to you alone.
endings.reward: A bead-maker's friendship at Ahus and beads there at the maker's price; here, Milava is wary for good, and her rumours are closed to this merchant.

stories.reward: The count in skins and beads, a place on the trading bank, and the first writing silver, without paying the big house for the introduction.

stories.title: Bare blades
stories.summary: The dealer in the biggest house pays the white silver for one thing above all: Frankish sword blades, brought bare so that no toll man at home sees a hilt. Holmfast of Birka carries them; the old smith puts the hilts on. A Frisian who brings his own breaks the king's law at one end of the road and a friend's custom at the other.
stories.picture: Inside a soot-black smithy: a lean smith with a plaited beard sighting down a bare sword blade held to the forge light, a small horned bronze figure on the shelf above him, and in the doorway a heavy man in a fur-lined cap holding a folding scale with thin coins in one pan.

beats.text: A blade may be sold to a count's man and to no stranger. A dealer who asks no questions will sell them bare, without hilt or guard, and wants silver by weight. Bare, he says, they are only iron bars with a good edge.
What lies under the ballast is between you and the toll man. He remembers a boat that sat lower than her cargo said.
Holmfast will buy every blade at Birka, for silver, at once, and carry them east himself. He says the lake beyond is no water for a boat your size. He says it twice.
Audvald bends one of your blades against his knee, lets it spring, and looks down it. He says nothing about where it came from. He asks whether you want hilts on them or want to be gone quickly.
Vigmund pays in the writing silver and does not make you wait. Then he asks, friend to friend, whether Holmfast knows you are here.

The Gotlanders take blades east in their own hulls, sworn at the ring and asking nobody at Birka. Vigmund cannot tell what they carry or what they bring home, and it troubles him more than Holmfast's counting ever did.

endings.how: You sold the blades to Holmfast at Birka and let him carry them east.
endings.text: A fair price and no risk on the lake. When you come to the Volkhov later, Vigmund already knows your name as the Frisian the blades come from, and Holmfast has said you can be trusted. It costs you a third of what the blades fetch here.
endings.reward: Holmfast as a friend (the thread's flag sw_buyer_known); a welcome at the big house; no deed against the king's law past the Danes' border.

endings.how: You carried the blades to Aldeigja yourself, had Audvald hilt them and sold them to Vigmund.
endings.text: Three times the Rhine price, in white silver, and a timber of marten thrown in. Audvald keeps one hilt pattern for your blades alone. Holmfast hears of it within the season. He does not quarrel; he recounts, and from then on he counts you among the people he competes with.
endings.reward: The best price on the road, paid in silver and furs; Vigmund and Audvald as friends; the thread's flags sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; Holmfast cools toward the house until a gift mends it.

endings.how: You refused to carry arms and told Vigmund so to his face.
endings.text: He hears you out and is not offended. A man who will not sell him swords will not sell them to his enemies either, he says, and that is worth something. He buys your cloth instead, at a fair weight, and tells Audvald, who for once has an opinion: he approves.
endings.reward: Nothing in silver. Aldger's heart rises if he is aboard; Audvald's riddle is given without the usual wait; no mark against the house anywhere in the west.

stories.reward: The eastern end of the sword road: either Holmfast's friendship or the best price on it, and the smith's regard whichever is chosen.

stories.title: A corpse on a corpse
stories.summary: The old smith saw something go down the river on the spring ice and has made a riddle of it. Whoever answers is told where a small bag of the first writing silver was put in the ground when he was a young man, by someone who never came back for it. In a later age the same river gives the tale of a prince, a horse and a snake.
stories.picture: A wide brown river in thaw seen from the top of a steep grassy mound: grey ice floes turning in the current, and on one of them the dark shape of a dead horse, a crow sitting on its ribs; small figures on the bank below shading their eyes.

beats.text: The smith sets it while he works: an earth-dweller passing by, a corpse sitting on a corpse, a blind one riding a blind sea-car, and the steed lifeless. He will not hear an answer the same day.

Budimir, asked what goes down the river at ice-break, counts on his fingers: trees, a sledge, once a whole fish trap, a cow. And every spring some horse that went through the ice in winter, riding its floe to the lake.
A skald in the Danes' hall knows the riddle and the wording, and says it is one of Gestumblindi's. He adds a line the smith did not give: in some mouths there is a snake on the dead horse too.
With the answer given, the smith walks you to the mounds and stands on a spot between two of them. Here, he says. A man with a spade and a quiet evening. He goes back to his forge without watching.

In a later age the tallest mound has a name, and a tale: a prince was told his horse would be his death, and sent it away; years on he set his foot on its skull to laugh, and a snake came out of it. The riddle's snake has found its horse.

On Gotland they remember the smith's kin, and the winter a grey Dane sat a bench with one of them. A skipper says the same riddle is asked on that beach, of the spring ice in the lagoon, and with a dead sheep.

endings.how: You answered the riddle, dug by night and kept what you found.
endings.text: A rotted bag, and in it some thirty thin coins, the youngest struck seven summers before you first sailed. Nobody claims them. The smith asks only how many, nods at the number, and says the man who buried them counted the same.
endings.reward: The small hoard (riddles_793.json rw_hoard_ladoga): white silver by weight, about a mark; the smith's regard.

endings.how: You dug, and laid a tenth of it at the foot of the nearest mound before you left.
endings.text: The smith watches this time. He says the ground here is full of people who were promised something. From then on, when your boat is in, there is a fresh mark on the tally stick by his forge that is not a debt.
endings.reward: The hoard less a tenth; the smith as a fast friend, and repairs at his forge at the cost of the iron; the people of the place speak well of the house (the deed fair_dealing).

endings.how: You answered, were shown the place, and did not dig.
endings.text: The smith is silent for a time, and then tells you the rest: who buried it, and why he did not come back. It is not a story with silver in it. The coins lie there until a spade finds them eleven hundred years later.
endings.reward: No silver. The smith's whole account of the first Northmen here, and a second riddle to carry west; Ravn, if aboard, says it was the right answer to the second question.

stories.reward: The oldest silver on the east road, or the story of the man who left it, and a smith who will ask you a harder one next time.

stories.title: Ash on the Volkhov
stories.summary: About 865 the town is burned to the ground. A ship that comes up the river for furs finds charred posts, nobody to weigh with, trappers who do not know whom to sell to, and a boy digging with his father where they think the family silver lies. What the merchant does that summer decides whether anyone here remembers his house when the town is built again.
stories.picture: A river bank of black stumps and grey ash under a hard blue sky: a man and a boy of ten digging between charred house posts, a single sea ship with her mast down at the mouth of a side river, and far off on the bank three men in fur caps waiting beside bundles of skins.

beats.text: The fort at the stream mouth is shut and half empty. A man on the wall shouts that the town is gone and that he does not know who did it. He asks whether you have food to sell, not what you have come to buy.

Charred posts, a few lean-tos, the smell of wet ash. Nobody comes down to the boat. A man and a boy are digging where a house stood. The man says his father put the silver under the threshold. They have found the threshold.
The trappers have come as they always do and stand with their bundles on an empty bank. There is no scale in the place but yours, and no one to say what a skin is worth but you.
At Birka they have heard, and are not surprised. A man there will sell you timber, tools and salt meat for the east on credit, at a rate that says what he thinks of your chances.
The town stands again. The boy who dug is a man with a house on the Northmen's street, and either he looks up when your boat comes round the bend, or he does not.

beats.when: year >= 865 and year < 871 and (flag.be_ash_fair or flag.be_ash_hard)
beats.text: Two Gotland boats came home early and light, and their skippers say only that the river town was ash and they did not stay. By the frost the whole west shore knows what a timber of marten cost there that summer, and who paid it.

endings.how: You bought the trappers' furs at the price of the year before, with nobody there to hold you to it, and helped the man dig.
endings.text: You could have had the furs for a third. The trappers know it. The man and the boy find a blackened lump of silver on the fourth day and try to give you half; you take a tenth. When the big house is built in 881 its host is that boy, and he knows your father's boat.
endings.reward: Hallstein as a fast friend from 881, inherited at half as always: a bench in the big house for nothing (lodge), and the unlock aldeigjuborg.bench; the trappers bring this house the winter fur first for a generation.

endings.how: You bought the furs for what desperate men would take, and sailed.
endings.text: The best cargo your house ever carried out of the east, for the least silver. Nobody on the bank says anything. Sixteen years later the host of the big house serves you civilly, charges you the full price, and never once asks after your father.
endings.reward: Three times the usual profit on one cargo of furs. From 881 Hallstein is cool toward the house, and rumours here cost a drink each.

endings.how: You went back to Birka and returned before the frost with timber, tools and food (the work aldeigjuborg.work.timber).
endings.text: Yours is the first roof raised on the burned bank, and four families winter under it. The Northmen who rebuild the town keep that house standing where it is and build their street past its door.
endings.reward: The work aldeigjuborg.work.timber done: a plot on the Northmen's street that is the house's own, with a store, and the friendship of the place for two generations.

stories.reward: A name on the Volkhov that outlasts the fire: a host who knows the house, or a roof of its own on the new street.

stories.title: The black stone
stories.summary: In 997 Jarl Eirik Hakonarson comes over the lake with warships, shuts the town in its stone fort and burns it after a long siege. A merchant in the river when the sails are seen can run for the lake, carry people out, or sell to whoever is winning. Twenty-two years later a Svea jarl sits in the rebuilt fort and asks every western skipper where his house stood that summer.
stories.picture: A grey dry-stone fort on a point between two rivers at dusk, smoke pouring from behind its wall; long low warships drawn up on the bank below with shields along the rail, and a small trading boat pulling away downstream, crowded with women and bundles.

beats.text: A fisherman rows up from the lake hard, shouting. Long ships, many, coming on the north wind with their masts down. The men in the fort begin hauling goods up through the hatch in the river wall. You have until they reach the bend.

From inside the wall a man calls down that the fort will take your cargo and your crew's arms, at any price you name, payable when the Northmen have gone. From the bank, townspeople hold children up toward your boat.
At the old stream mouth, long empty, Eirik's ships lie on the mud. A man of his asks whether you have ale, meat and rope, and offers silver that was somebody else's a week ago.
Jarl Ragnvald walks you along the foot of the wall and shows you the stone, black to head height. He asks where your house stood that summer. He already knows; he wants to hear how you tell it.

In the Svear king's new town they say the jarl in the east holds the river town as the bride-gift of the king's daughter, and takes no tenth there. Merchants who have been say the gift at the fort comes to much the same.

A Gotlander at the new quays was on the eastern river the year the jarl's ships came, and saw the stone burn black to head height. He says the fort took every arrow he carried and paid when the ships had gone, which was more than he expected.

endings.how: You threw cargo on the bank and carried townspeople across the lake.
endings.text: You lose most of a hold of furs and bring nineteen people out alive. Some come back when the fort is rebuilt in timber. Under the jarl their children are householders, and one of them is the man who takes the mooring rope of every ship that comes in.
endings.reward: The cargo lost. From the early 1000s the house lies at the best berth without asking (ask_harbour, careen and repair at the townsmen's price); Ragnvald, hearing it, gives the house the unlock aldeigjuborg.jarls_peace.

endings.how: You sent your cargo up through the hatch on the fort's promise to pay.
endings.text: The fort burns with your goods in it. Nobody is left who made the promise. But the debt was witnessed, and in 1019 the jarl, who is careful about such things, pays a third of it from the princess's dues and calls it closed.
endings.reward: A third of the cargo's worth, twenty-two years late, and the jarl's respect for a house that keeps its tallies (the unlock aldeigjuborg.jarls_peace).

endings.how: You sold ale, meat and rope to the jarl's ships.
endings.text: Good silver, paid at once. Eirik's men are civil to a useful stranger. When Ragnvald asks in 1019 where your house stood, you can lie, and he will know, or tell him, and he will thank you for the truth and seat you below the salt for as long as he holds the town.
endings.reward: Silver now, and a safe passage down the lake through Eirik's ships. Under the jarls the house pays a larger gift at the fort and is last to be given a berth.

stories.reward: Standing with the jarls of Aldeigjuborg in the last age, earned or lost in one week of 997.

works.name: A log store on the bank
works.what: A cabin of notched logs on a stone footing with a turf roof, a plank floor raised off the damp and a door barred from inside, built by local men in the local way. Skins hang from the rafters and wax lies below.
works.needs: Vigmund at least friendly, or the silver road ended with ground of your own here (the flag unlock_plot_aldeigjuborg); a call after midsummer, when the builders are back from the river.
works.gives: Store a full hold here over the winter: furs bought at the snow price wait for your boat at ice-break. If Folkbern is the house's man he keeps the key, and buys for you through the winter.
works.picture: A new log cabin with pale notched corners and a turf roof on a muddy river bank, bundles of furs being passed in through its low door, a slight fair-haired man in grey cutting a notch in a tally stick beside it.
works.source: works_793.json storehouse. Log cabins are how the place was built from the 760s (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 1). No Frisian house on the Volkhov is known (Design/content/chains/silver_road.md): the work is invented.

works.name: A share in a river boat
works.what: A third share in a long shallow boat that goes above the rapids, with her pilot and six men, for one season up to the upper lake and back. Your goods go where your hull cannot.
works.needs: The pilot of the river at least easy with you; goods to send, and somebody you trust to go with them or the patience to trust the pilot.
works.gives: Once a season, a cargo of yours is sold up the river at the inland price and its return brought down before the frost: furs and wax in the early years, silver in the best ones. Doubtful in the years of war on the river.
works.picture: A long, low, plank-sided river boat being poled up brown water between limestone banks, bales amidships under hides, a short wide-shouldered pilot standing in the bow with a sounding pole.
works.source: works_793.json ship_share. Goods go on from here by river boat (de.wikipedia 'Staraja Ladoga'; realms/rus.json road north 2-3). The terms of a share are invented in the manner of later northern partnership (?).

works.name: Timber for the burned bank
works.what: A cargo of squared pine, iron tools, nails and salt meat brought from Birka before the frost, and the first roof raised on the ash: one long house that four families winter under.
works.needs: The story 'Ash on the Volkhov' begun; a hold big enough for timber, or two voyages.
works.gives: A plot and a store on the Northmen's street that is the house's own from 870, and the good will of the town for two generations: lodging, berth and news for nothing.
works.picture: Men raising the frame of a long house among charred stumps on a river bank, fresh yellow timber against black ash, a sea ship unloading planks at the water's edge, first snow in the air.
works.source: The burning of about 865 and the rebuilding (ru.wikipedia 'Старая Ладога'; dossier 5); works_793.json plot. The merchant's part is invented.

works.name: A length of the stone wall
works.what: Flagstone quarried from the river bank, carried and laid dry for ten paces of the new fort's river wall, with your mark cut on one stone at the foot. The lord's men build the rest.
works.needs: A gift already given at the fort; a bench in the big house.
works.gives: A corner of the fort's store for your goods, hoisted through the river hatch and under the lord's guard (store); a hearing at the fort without waiting (audience). Your stone is there to be found in every later age, black after 997.
works.picture: A half-built wall of grey flat stones laid without mortar on a point above a brown river, men passing slabs up a ramp, a square opening high in the wall with a beam and rope, and at the foot a man cutting a mark into one stone.
works.source: works_793.json wall_share. The stone fort of about 900: flagstone without mortar, about 8 m high, a loading hatch 7 m up the river wall (ru.wikipedia 'Староладожская крепость'; dossier 2). Who paid for it is not recorded: a merchant's share is invented (?).

works.name: A mound on the far bank
works.what: A man of your house or crew who dies in the east is laid on the far bank and a small mound is raised over him: turf cut by hired hands, a ring of stones at the foot. Burned first if he was a heathen; laid whole with his head to the west if he was not.
works.needs: A death aboard or in the town; the leave of whoever holds the fort, which a gift buys.
works.gives: The crew's heart is steadied, and the town's Northmen count your house as one that has dead here: a standing no silver buys otherwise. An heir who climbs it can remember (remember).
works.picture: A low new mound of cut turf on a river terrace among older grassed mounds, a ring of pale stones round its foot, four men with spades resting, the town's roofs and a fort small across the wide water behind.
works.source: works_793.json grave_stone. Plakun: mounds from about 850, cremations early, a chamber grave of a man perhaps Christian, unmounded Christian graves in the 1000s (ru.wikipedia 'Плакун (урочище)'; dossier 2, 6). A western merchant's man buried there is invented.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The river boat of the Northmen here: clinker-built, light, four or five pairs of oars, made to be carried round rocks on men's shoulders. The pine is cut in winter and the boat is ready at ice-break. It is the only hull of yours that will ever see the upper river.
ships.picture: A slim new clinker boat on trestles outside a soot-black smithy, snow on the ground, a smith driving a rivet while a boy holds the rove, the brown river iced over behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat (lake and river boat); ship rivets at the Lyubsha fort and in the town (ru.wikipedia 'Любшанская крепость'; dossier 2, 3); goods go on by river boat (dossier 4).

ships.note: A dugout of aspen or pine, paddled by one or two, for the side streams and for getting ashore across the mud. Any householder on the small river has one too many and will sell it for a knife or a few ounces of salt.
ships.picture: A narrow dugout nosed into reeds at the mouth of a small river, a paddle and a fish spear lying in her, a barefoot man in a long linen shirt holding the bow.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_logboat (to be had at aldeigjuborg). The wood is a guess (?).

ships.note: A big dugout widened with a plank a side: the Slavs' and Finns' freight boat for the rapids, hired with her crew for the run above the rocks. She carries two tons of wax or skins and comes back when the pilot says she will.
ships.picture: A long dugout with a raised plank along each side, loaded with yellow wax cakes and poled by four men through broken water between rocks.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat_expanded; boats of planks sewn or added to a log among the Finns and Slavs are not checked for this river (?) (peoples/baltic_east.md 6).

ships.note: A Svea sea ship of twelve to eighteen metres left at the landing against a debt, or by a crew that went up the river and did not come down. The big house, and later the fort, sells such a ship for silver by weight to a man who can bring his own crew for her.
ships.picture: A broad clinker-built ship with her mast lowered, lying alone on the mud at a river mouth, weed on her waterline, a heavy man in a fur-lined cap pointing at her with a folding scale in his other hand.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship: the sea ships that stop here (peoples/baltic_east.md 6); 'the ship left for a debt' is the silver road chain's own invention (Design/content/chains/silver_road.md).

sayings.text: Our whole land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us.
sayings.source: The Chuds and Slavs to the Varangians, under the year 862: the Russian Primary Chronicle, tr. Samuel H. Cross (Harvard Studies and Notes in Philology and Literature 12, 1930), as given in Design/content/peoples/baltic_east.md 8. Written about 1113 of a year long before; to be said here only from the 870s, and with a straight face.

sayings.text: May we become yellow as gold, and be slain with our own weapons.
sayings.source: The heathen Rus oath on a treaty, under the year 971: the Russian Primary Chronicle, tr. Cross 1930, as given in peoples/baltic_east.md 8. What a man says at the posts before he gives his hand on a bargain, from the 870s.

sayings.text: Not a mere washing but a veritable torment.
sayings.source: Of the steam baths of the Novgorod country, where men lash themselves with switches until half dead and then pour cold water over themselves: the Russian Primary Chronicle, tr. Cross 1930, as given in peoples/baltic_east.md 9. Said by any westerner who has been talked into the bath-house.

sayings.text: Away from his arms in the open field / A man should fare not a foot; / For never he knows when the need for a spear / Shall arise on the distant road.
sayings.source: Hávamál 38, tr. Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), as given in Design/content/lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj011. The Northmen's rule on the river road.

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, / And so one dies one's self; / But a noble name will never die, / If good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Hávamál 77, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj019). Said under the tall mounds, whose names nobody remembers.

sayings.text: I saw an earth-dweller pass by, a corpse sitting on a corpse; a blind one riding on a blind sea-car, yet the steed was lifeless.
sayings.source: Gestumblindi's riddle 24, from the saga of King Heidrek, tr. Gudbrand Vigfusson and F. York Powell, Corpus Poeticum Boreale (1883): texts_793.json t-gest-24. The smith's riddle; the answer is a dead horse on an ice floe.

sayings.text: The Frank asks what a thing costs. The Svea asks what it weighs. Here they ask how many skins, and then they ask the woman.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a trader's turn on three reckonings: the spine's silver_road)

sayings.text: Nobody takes a toll at Aldeigja. You only give a gift to everybody.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a Northman's understatement); no toll is known here (Design/content/audit/ports.md)

sayings.text: The lake has no tide, so it has to drown you some other way.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; said by Frisians. The lake: shoals along the south shore and steep seas in a wind (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md)

sayings.text: He prayed to the post for a buyer who would not haggle. The post sent him a Svea.
sayings.source: invented joke in the period's manner, on the Rus traders' prayer as an envoy of the caliph heard it on the Volga in 922 (Ibn Fadlan, in paraphrase: peoples/baltic_east.md 5) and on the Svea who counts everything twice (BRIEF.md tone guide). From about 900.

easter_eggs.text: On the shelf over the smith's door sits a bronze man as long as a finger with two horns curving up from his head. The smith calls it the singer. It is the top of some older thing, cast in the Northmen's style of his grandfather's day, and the horns are a head-dress on a figure. Ask anyone here whether men wear such a thing and they will ask what for.
